title: Payment validation (Cloudflare Monetization Gateway docs)
notes: Read 2026-11-14 through the .md twin (HTTP 200, 2026-11-15T04:58Z UTC). The page was last updated 2026-09-30 (dateModified 2026-09-30), so this text predates the 2026-10-11 check of the orbit page. The origin receives the payment authorization as a JWT in a PAYMENT-CONTEXT header and must verify it (Ed25519, pinned JWKS at https://payments.cloudflare.com/certs) before serving paid content. Fixed pricing uses the x402 exact scheme and settles the signed amount. Variable pricing uses upto: the JWT carries the authorized maximum, and after a successful response the origin sets a PAYMENT-SETTLEMENT header with the actual amount. Above the maximum the gateway settles the maximum, at zero nothing is settled, and the gateway removes PAYMENT-SETTLEMENT from the response sent to the buyer.

title: Amazon.com Conditions of Use (Agents section)
notes: Read 2026-11-14 (HTTP 200, 2026-11-15T04:48Z UTC); page last updated 2026-08-14. The Agents section (Agent Terms; added 2025-05-30 per the First Amended Complaint, paragraph 29) applies to anyone who uses, allows, enables or causes the deployment of an Agent, meaning software that acts autonomously or semi-autonomously for a person. An Agent must identify itself at all times, may not access Amazon Services if Amazon has asked it to refrain, must put Agent/[agent name] in the user agent string of every HTTP request, must not mimic human keystrokes or navigation or complete or circumvent CAPTCHAs, must answer truthfully whether it is a human or a computer, and must not circumvent measures that limit agent access. The identification is a self-declared string, not a cryptographic signature. Re-read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200): still marked Last updated: August 14, 2026, with the Agents section in place.

title: Sybil Resistance in Reputations for Agentic Marketplaces
notes: Read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200; page dated November 13, 2026; authors Reza Ramji, Preston Vander Vos and Duc Le of Circle Research). Introduces Anduin, which rates x402 service providers from the payment graph (who pays whom), so that to look trusted to an agent an attacker must spend real money at the services that agent already uses. Circle says that on 66 million real x402 payments (66.1 million settlements worth $6.1 million over 157 days, 2026-03-23 to 2026-08-26, on 16 networks: 15 EVM chains and Solana) Anduin recommends providers about as accurately as the best standard method, collaborative filtering, which it does not beat on accuracy, while being about 23 times more expensive to manipulate in the tested attack; it needs no change to x402, HTTP payment headers or ERC standards. Circle also says fewer than 4,000 voluntary on-chain ratings (for example ERC-8004 feedback) were recorded across those payments. The post notes that Circle Research projects are not completed or released software or services. Research paper: arXiv 2611.05586 (src-orbit-circle-anduin-arxiv).

title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system
notes: Abstract page read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200). Reza Ramji, Preston Vander Vos, Ziming Zeng and Duc V. Le; primary category cs.AI; only v1 (Tue, 3 Nov 2026 20:17:03 UTC). The abstract models payment flows as a bipartite graph between buyers and providers over a 157-day dataset of 66 million agentic transactions worth $6.1 million on 16 blockchains, proposes three Sybil-resistant ratings, and reports that against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers rating manipulation costs 20 percent of those buyers' total spend, about 23 times harder than collaborative filtering. Library entry pub-ramji-2026-anduin.

title: Introducing Menta: Open-Source Plugin for Agentic Commerce
notes: Read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200; JSON-LD datePublished and dateModified 2026-11-18). Menta is an open-source agentic commerce plugin built on Crossmint's Agent Commerce Toolkit (launched in October) that lets an AI assistant buy for its user. It is in the ChatGPT, Devin and Grok Bot plugin marketplaces; for Claude, Muse and other assistants the user pastes a setup prompt from menta.crossmint.com. The card stays in a PCI-compliant vault and the assistant never sees the number; the user approves a spending limit and how long it lasts, or approves every purchase. Menta checks out through the store's own API, an agent protocol or a browser built for checkout, names no protocol, accepts cards issued around the world, and pays with the user's own card (the post says no one-time virtual cards) or a card saved in the store account, Shop Pay, Pix or Bizum. Crossmint says that in its test at 3,000 stores Menta completed 91 percent of purchases, 5 to 10 times faster than general-purpose agents using browser checkouts, and warns that it will not get every store right yet. The post states no price.
